HOMES, GARDENS & CULTURAL TRADITIONS

Many journeys. Different cultures. One shared history.

People came to Hawaiʻi from across Asia, Europe, the Pacific and the Americas, bringing languages, foods, faiths, celebrations, skills and memories of home.

At the Village, historic homes, community spaces, artifacts and gardens reveal how families lived, worked, celebrated and built community across generations.

Step inside. Look closely. Every home has a unique story to tell.

THE VILLAGE

History has a home here.

Hawaii's Plantation Village was created by visionaries who understood that an important part of Hawaii's story could disappear if no one chose to preserve it.

Beginning in the 1970s, former plantation workers, descendants and community members came together to save the buildings, belongings, photographs, gardens and memories of plantation life.

Rather than telling these stories from a distance, they helped create a place where future generations could walk through a living museum.

Today, visitors can enter historic homes and community structures, encounter objects from everyday life and explore our lush gardens with a plethora of local foods and plants connected to the unique plantation cultures represented here.

Our docents bring these stories to life through animated anecdotes of work and hardship, family and faith, struggle and solidarity, celebration and change.

Together, we experience how people from diverse regions helped shape the Hawaiʻi we know today.

OKADA EDUCATION CENTER

Where memory becomes history.

Every photograph has a story. Every object carries a memory. Together, these help us understand lives that may otherwise be forgotten.

The Okada Education Center is named after Hideo “Major” Okada, a former sugar worker, labor organizer and one of the founders of Hawaii's Plantation Village.

Here, visitors explore exhibitions on immigration, plantation life and labor, as well as the history of World War II incarceration at Honouliuli.

Behind the scenes, volunteers care for a growing collection of photographs, documents and artifacts donated by families across Hawaiʻi.

These are not simply records of the past but treasured pieces of familial history, entrusted to us for the future.

FOR EDUCATORS & STUDENTS

History feels different when you experience it

Bring learning beyond the classroom.

At Hawaii's Plantation Village, students enter historic homes, explore cultural gardens, encounter everyday objects and hear stories that connect Hawaiʻi's plantation era to the islands they know today.

Guided experiences invite students to explore migration, labor, cultural exchange, family, community and change through the lives of real people.

A visit can complement classroom learning before, during and after your field trip and give students something no textbook can: a sense of place.

Hawaii's Plantation Village exists because generations of people knew these stories mattered.

You can help us carry this important work forward.

VOLUNTEER

History needs people – YOU.

The Village exists because people showed up.

They preserved buildings, donated family photographs, planted gardens, recorded memories, led tours, made repairs and shared traditions.

This spirit continues today.

Whether you love history, gardening, education, archives, cultural programs or simply working with the community, there is a place for you at Hawaii's Plantation Village.

You do not need to be a historian. You just need to care that these stories survive.

THE VILLAGE GROUNDS

Buildings from Hawaiʻi's plantation camps.

What you will experience at Hawaii's Plantation Village is an overview of plantation buildings that could be found on many sugar plantations throughout Hawaiʻi in the early 1900s.

The Village is not laid out as a typical campsite. Camps were often a close cluster of small, square, three-room structures with their front doors facing each other, and a narrow road winding down the center. Here, a barber shop, community furo, infirmary, garage, store, camp office and social/union hall give you an impression of the other buildings that were part of the plantation setting.

Each home is furnished with items that reflect its ethnic group from around 1900 to the late 1930s, and each is set for a day that group selected. The Filipino family home is set for a baptismal party, and the Japanese Christian home is set for bible study.

The Hawaiian Hale & Taro Patch

INSIDE THE HOME

Hawaiian life at the Village

Long before contract laborers arrived, Native Hawaiian families cultivated the ahupuaʻa of Waipahu, tending loʻi kalo (taro patches) fed by the ʻauwai (irrigation channels) that later shaped the plantation's own ditch system. As the sugar era grew, Hawaiian families remained woven into camp life — teaching neighbors to fish, pound poi, and read the land — even as their own community was reshaped by the plantation around them.

At the Village: Hālau Waʻa & Hawaiian Hale Moe (1850) · Loʻi Kalo

“My tūtū kept the loʻi going even after the ditch water was diverted for cane. She said the taro remembered this valley long before the mill whistle ever did. Workers from every camp came to trade for poi, and she taught their children the names of the wind and rain here. The plantation changed everything around us, but the kalo kept us rooted.”

A Sweeter Scent of Hope

Migration, family and community

INSIDE THE HOME

Chinese life at the Village

Chinese laborers arrived starting in 1852 as the first major group of contract workers. Gathering in camp cookhouses, they preserved traditional culinary practices while exchanging recipes with other cultures, establishing the foundational roots of Hawaiʻi's unique, blended local cuisine.

At the Village: Chinese Society Building (1909)

I still remember the day our ship arrived in Hawaiʻi. After weeks at sea, the endless blue ocean gave way to green mountains rising from the mist. The air smelled different—sweet, warm, and filled with the scent of tropical flowers. For a moment, I forgot why I had come. Back home, opportunities were scarce. My family struggled to survive, and every season brought more uncertainty. When I heard stories of work in Hawaiʻi, I knew I had to take the chance. It wasn't an easy decision. Leaving meant saying goodbye to my parents, my friends, and the life I had always known. But I carried one hope with me—that my sacrifices would build a better future.
SAN JOE

PORTUGUESE · ARRIVED 1878

Portuguese Plantation Food Traditions & Family Memories

Family, food, faith and celebration

All homes

INSIDE THE HOME

Portuguese life at the Village

Oral history interviewee shares memories of traditional Portuguese recipes passed down through generations. Key dishes mentioned include vinha d'alhos (pickled pork), Portuguese sweet bread baked in a backyard brick oven, homemade Portuguese sausage, pickled onions, and bacalhau (dried salt codfish) fried with chili peppers, onions, and vinegar served alongside poi with shoyu. The account highlights weekly family meal schedules and cooking routines before modern refrigeration.

At the Village: Portuguese House (1918) · Portuguese Forno

Interviewer: What was your kind of your favorite foods growing up as a kid? Man: Food... traditional things. Christmas was always the pickled pork, vinha d'alhos. It's like pork adobo, Filipino style, except Portuguese style, which is more chili pepper in it. It's a little different. And sweet bread, of course. Sweet bread was always a wonderful thing because my grandmother made it and baked it in the backyard. We had a brick oven. I remember at Christmas, her baking sweet bread. At the time, you didn't go out to the market and buy sweet bread. Even Portuguese sausage, my grandmother made maybe once a year. It was hard work, it was difficult. And so we only got it maybe once a year. And pickled onions. Now everything's refrigerated. We never used to refrigerate. Now everybody tells you, "You've got to put it in the refrigerator afterwards." That's the kind of things that, you know, Portuguese-related stuff. It was all, you know, it wasn't much of store-bought stuff back then, yeah. It was all homemade. Dried codfish, bacalhau. And Friday was fish day for us. So, my mother would fry the dried bacalhau. She'd soak it first, of course, to reconstitute it, and fry it with chili pepper and onions and vinegar. But I remembered it was always chewy. So I remember chewing and chewing, but we always had it with poi. And I learned to eat poi with shoyu in it. Interviewer: Poi with shoyu? Man: Instead of milk or sugar. Interviewer: Nice. Man: And that's how I learned to eat it. Because, and even today, I'll put shoyu in my poi. Well, I pickled onions. So I used the pickled onions and I put it in the poi. Once in a while, something cold, instead of cooking. And Wednesday was soup day. Every Wednesday would be a different soup. It could be Portuguese-style bean soup, any vegetables that were around. It could be taro in it, it could be pumpkin in it with the cabbages and, you know, and other times it might be a thin broth, tomato broth with some pasta in it. Saturday was the big meal of the day because my mother worked. So Saturday was a roast or pork chops or something like that. Sunday was a day of rest, so a dinner might... Usually breakfast, she would cook us breakfast. We'd all sit at the dinner—at the table. Sundays, bacon and eggs, muffins. We'd go to Pearl City for the muffins after church, pick them up. It was near, on the way to the Pearl City Tavern. And then lunch is something simple: tuna sandwich and chips or something. And then dinner was something simple, too. Might be hamburgers and buns with pork and beans or something. Monday was leftover sandwiches for school—school lunch of what we had on Saturday. So they always made perfect sandwiches: roast beef or pork, like that. And so those were the special days for certain foods.

JAPANESE · ARRIVED 1900

Japanese-American Agricultural Experience at Camp Amache

Home, work, faith and tradition

All homes

INSIDE THE HOME

Japanese life at the Village

Official War Relocation Authority (WRA) records show that by summer 1943, evacuees had cleared over 500 acres of prairie land surrounding the camp. Utilizing traditional Japanese farming techniques combined with modern irrigation practices, the camp community produced over 30 varieties of vegetables—including daikon, napa cabbage, and celery—supplying both Camp Amache and neighboring internment centers with fresh produce.

At the Village: Japanese Duplex (1910) · Wakamiya Inari Shrine (1914) · Japanese Christian House (1930s) · Tofu-ya · Community Furo

The siding on these barracks is warped now, another layer of paint peeled back by the sun. But out past the treeline, where the dust hangs gold, you can still trace the lines of the furrows we dug. The earth was so stubborn, packed hard as clay. We broke it with iron, with hope, and with hand. That rusted old valve at the head of the ditch—it was the first heart that beat in this barren land. We planted our roots here, a defiant green promise, turnin' this dust into somethin' that felt like a home.
KENJI TAKAHASHI (BORN 1928, LOS ANGELES, CA)

The Okinawan Sanshin & Prefectural Club

Identity, memory and community

All homes

INSIDE THE HOME

Okinawan life at the Village

Okinawan contract laborers arrived in Hawaiʻi in 1900, bringing a distinct Ryukyuan language, culture, and musical heritage. Settling in camp clusters, they maintained strong prefectural networks called sonjinkai. They introduced agricultural practices, pig farming, and traditional foods like andagi. The three-stringed sanshin became a cornerstone of plantation community music.

At the Village: Okinawan House (1919)

“My father made his first sanshin using an empty cigar box and a piece of eucalyptus wood. In the evenings, when the field dust settled, he would play the old Ryukyuan folk songs. The music was different from the Japanese songs—it was warmer, and the neighbors from all the other camps would lean over the fences to listen. It made this red dirt feel a little bit like Okinawa.”
KAMA UYEHARA (THIRD-GENERATION SANSHIN INSTRUCTOR)

COLLECTIONS & ARCHIVES

What families saved, Hawaiʻi remembers.

Photographs tucked into albums. Letters carried across oceans. Work tools worn smooth by use. Clothing saved for decades. Objects from kitchens, bedrooms and places of worship. Individually, they may seem ordinary. Together, they tell an extraordinary story.

THREE COLLECTIONS

Photograph collections

Hawaii's Plantation Village cares for photographs, documents, artifacts and oral histories that preserve the experiences of plantation communities across generations. Knowing who kept an image, and why, changes how you read it.

Oahu Sugar Company
Mainly from the 1940s to 1950s: sugar cane cultivation and harvesting, finances, mill operations, water systems, housing, and medical services. R.H. “Harry” Lodge, division overseer, and Ernest Malterre, Jr., housing supervisor, are credited for most of the collection. Lodge’s photographs of Honouliuli Internment Camp remain a constant resource for researchers.
2 DIGITIZED
Murakoshi Collection
Mae Okada’s collection of father-and-son photographers Nobunosuke and Henry Murakoshi. Nobunosuke’s photographs are primarily studio work; Henry’s give a peek into everyday Waipahu — school activities, picnics, celebrations, community events, camp homes, businesses, and locations.
0 DIGITIZED
Friends of Waipahu Cultural Garden Park
The largest collection in the HPV Photograph Archives: individual donations of family, work culture, WWII induction, group photos, education and recreation from plantation life. There is some overlap with Lodge, Malterre, and Nobunosuke Murakoshi. Includes panoramic class pictures, graduations, recognition and awards, and funeral photos.

LOOKING AT PHOTOGRAPHS

Questions that open an image

When viewing and interacting with photographs from the archives, these questions help develop a broader understanding of the image. All one needs is more context.

STEP 1
What does one see?
What are you able to identify in the image to indicate who or what is being captured in the photograph?
STEP 2
When or where?
Is there anything in the photograph that indicates when or where the photograph was taken?
STEP 3
Match, reinforce, or conflict?
Does the photograph match, reinforce, or conflict with your own knowledge of what has been captured in the image?
STEP 4
How do the elements interact?
Finally, how do the elements identified in the image interact with each other?

Analyze a photograph

WORKED EXAMPLES

How related frames build context

The study guide reads plantation-era prints with accession cards and backs. Use the same method on the digitized village slides below: observe first, then ask what a second frame confirms or complicates.

SAMPLE 1

Outside, then inside the same house
Dark camp cottage with white porch
Furnished camp interior opening to the lanai

In the study guide, Sample 1 uses metadata — filing category, subject, donor, accession year — and clues such as vehicles to date an undated street scene. Here, an exterior and an interior of camp housing work the same way: read what is visible in each frame, then ask what the pair can tell you that either image alone cannot.

SAMPLE 2

A building, then the people and objects inside it
Green cottage with red corrugated roof
Shiroma Saimin stand exhibit

Study Guide Sample 2 shows how a group event photograph can contradict assumptions — for example, that the Filipino community was primarily male by 1937. When people and named businesses appear in a frame, ask whether they are the subject or the evidence of when the shutter opened, and what the group composition challenges in your prior knowledge.

KEEP RESEARCHING

Resources for the photograph collections

A sample of online and library resources related to HPV’s photograph collections. This list is not exhaustive.

BYU Joseph F. Smith Library — Filipino Labor Collection

Special collections on Filipino laborers in Hawaiʻi.

Chinese, Japanese, and Portuguese passenger manifests; vital statistics 1826–1929; WWI service records.

Hawaii Sugar Planters Association records and related materials.

University of Hawaiʻi Press.

Odo, Voices from the Canefields (2013)

Poblete, Islanders in the Empire (2014)

Filipino and Puerto Rican laborers in Hawaiʻi. University of Illinois Press.

Kodama-Nishimoto et al., Talking Hawaiʻi’s Story (2009)

Oral histories of an island people. University of Hawaiʻi Press.

Koloa: an Oral History of a Kauaʻi Community (1988); The Closing of Sugar Plantations: Hamakua and Kaʻu (1997).

ABOUT HAWAII'S PLANTATION VILLAGE

Built by community. Preserved for generations.

Hawaii's Plantation Village began with a simple but urgent idea: don't let these stories disappear.

History and mission
Team
News
Careers
Contact
MISSION
What emerged was more than a collection. It became a Village.

In 1973, former plantation workers, descendants and community members began working to preserve the history of plantation life in Hawaiʻi.

Historic structures were gathered and restored. Families donated furniture, photographs and personal belongings. Cultural organizations helped furnish homes and plant gardens. Volunteers shared knowledge that could not always be found in history books.

Hawaii's Plantation Village opened to the public in 1992.

Today, we continue that community-led mission: preserving the places, objects and memories of Hawaiʻi's plantation era while creating opportunities for new generations to encounter, question and understand that history.

OUR MISSION

The Friends of Waipahu Cultural Garden Park, a non-profit educational organization, has as its purpose ensuring that the experiences, lifestyles, struggles, sacrifices, innovations and contributions of our plantation forebearers are known, acknowledged, and visible as the cornerstones of Hawaiʻi's successful multicultural society.

The Friends operate and maintain Hawaii's Plantation Village, a collection of historic and reconstructed plantation buildings and adjacent land, and the Okada Educational Center, an archival collection, exhibition, and classroom facility.

A living museum, for the people by the people.
CHRONICLES
From camps to village

Immigration waves that shaped plantation Hawaiʻi, and the founding of the Friends and the Village that tells their story.

1835

The first successful sugar plantation in Hawaiʻi gets its start in Kōloa, Kauaʻi. From the start, workers are paid not in cash but in coupons or scrip redeemable at the plantation store, and identified not by family name but by numbered metal bango tags.

1852

First waves of Chinese contract laborers arrive in Oʻahu aboard the Thetis, inaugurating the plantation era.

1868

The first group of Japanese workers arrives to work on Hawaiʻi's sugar plantations.

1875

The Reciprocity Treaty grants Hawaiʻi the right to export sugar duty-free to the United States. Together with demand from the 1848 California Gold Rush and the 1861 Civil War, it fuels the rapid expansion of Hawaiian sugar plantations.

1878

Portuguese workers arrive from Madeira and Azores, bringing stone ovens (forno) and the braguinha (ancestor of the ukulele).

1885

The Kanyaku Imin government-contract Japanese workers arrive, establishing major camp communities and furo baths.

1885

Plantations now provide workers housing, some food and medical care, with wages of $9 a month for men and $6 a month for women.

1897

Oahu Sugar Company is incorporated in Waipahu, erecting the massive sugar mill smokestack that dominated the skyline.

1900

Puerto Rican workers arrive, followed by Okinawan workers in the early 1900s.

1903

First Korean immigrants land in Honolulu, setting up language schools, programs, and active community organizations.

1906

The first Filipino sakadas arrive, recruited by the Hawaii Sugar Planters Association (HSPA), eventually forming the largest labor segment.

1910

Major Filipino immigration takes place, four years after the first Filipino workers arrived in 1906.

1973

The Friends of Waipahu Cultural Garden Park incorporate, founded by a former plantation worker and plantation-worker descendants committed to a village that would teach later generations their heritage.

1992

Hawaii's Plantation Village opens in Waipahu after a capital campaign led by executive director Cal Kawamoto raised over $2 million, with another $1 million from the State Legislature for the $2.5 million project.

Founders and builders
Hideo “Major” Okada
FOUNDER

Former sugar worker and labor union organizer; one of the village founders. The Okada Education Center is named in his honor.

Cal Kawamoto
EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR (CAPITAL CAMPAIGN)

Created the capital fund drive advisory committee and worked with ethnic historical groups to plan and furnish the village exhibits.

Spencer Leinweber
PRINCIPAL ARCHITECT

Of Spencer Mason Architecture; selected as principal architect for Hawaii's Plantation Village.

JOIN US
History lives when people engage with it.

Through exhibitions, guided tours, education, festivals, cultural programs, oral histories and community partnerships, we connect the past with the Hawaiʻi of today.

The Village was built so these stories would survive. Our responsibility now is to make sure they continue to matter.

It really does take a village — so do join us today.
